sections.title: Chairman's Chat
sections.content:
Tam reports

Happy New Year to one and all, here’s hoping for a great flying year for everyone in the Dales. We’ve turned the corner to a new year, and a new era for the club, the post Martin era. We wish him a happy retirement after his amazing tenure as Chair – it will surely never be equaled. As with all things in life though, we need to look forward and not backwards.  The 2025 AGM closed  with a gap on the committee, which was immediately filled before we left the room as Chris Fountain stepped forward to take on the role of PG Comps. Together with other new blood Jordan Whittaker (Library) and Simon Hulme (Airspace) we have a great blend of experience and enthusiasm to take the club forward and cope with the myriad of issues that always present themselves for the committee to deal with.  The aim of the club has always been to enable and promote safe flying in the Dales, and that will remain the focus. However, although the committee definitely has a role to play in that aim, it is the actions of individuals that actually delivers the results. So let’s all start the new year with reaffirming to ourselves that we will make good and safe flying decisions this year.

Promoting safe flying covers a wide remit. I was struck at the AGM with Chris Kay’s point about our role and actions in bringing new blood into our sport – without new blood we as a club and the sport in general is on a time limited trajectory.  This is a topic that the BHPA looked at and concluded that whilst important, it had no real answers. The DHPC committee also discussed it a couple of years ago, with no real conclusion (though we did contribute to the making of Kinga Masztalerz’ film “Soar” which promoted women’s participation in our sport).  We are fortunate to have some talented younger pilots in the club now, however I think we need to continue to grapple with this issue to identify if there are more things we can do to help to grow the sport and club. Thanks to Chris for raising this.  We as a committee would welcome ideas from members about this, or any other issues that you think we could be addressing.

On a personal level, having taken over as Chair I am tempted to think that the main thing that I am looking forward to is that I will clearly be due better fortune with my attempts at flying bigger XCs, with fantastic low saves,  never ending thermals, and decisions that always result in optimal results. Yes Tam, as if!

Have a great year everyone, fly safe.

sections.title: Safety, Reserve Repack and Hello from your new Safety Officer
sections.content:
Rob Urselmann reports

Reserve repack cancelled

Unfortunately, due to lack of interest, the club reserve repack that was planned for the 17th has been cancelled.

We are in communication with PSC who apparently are planning their repack on 1st March in Chipping. Once we have details these will be shared via the social media channels.

Update post-publish: PSC repack

PSC reserve repack 1st March 2026

Chipping village hall, Garstang Rd, Chipping, Preston PR3 2QH

The event will be split into a morning session 8.30 - 12.30, afternoon session 12.30 - 4.30

Plenty of availability for afternoon.

Cost  - £30

PSC contact: Barry Sayer <barrysayer72 @ gmail.com>

PSC Bank details:

Lloyds Bank

02650706 – account number

30-96-85 – sort code

Please use your full name as a reference on payment.

Hello

Hello to all as your new Safety Officer.  First off a BIG thank you to Clive who’s performed a stellar job in this role for I honestly don’t know how long.

Despite Clive’s extensive efforts, there was insufficient interest this year in pilots packing their own reserves under BHPA supervision. I am curious to know whether you pack your own or whether you send yours off for a professional repack, just please don’t tell me it’s been over a year since you had it pulled out, aired and repacked.

Now, our sport is known as an “extreme” sport and most of us know somebody (if not ourselves) who’ve had “prangs” and too many of us know people who sadly had fatal accidents. This past season has seen particular attention after three high-profile fatalities in the high-level competitions. In our own club, this last summer saw notable injuries on Dodd & Wether in August, and in 2024 we had at least three serious injuries (including my own) and the UK saw a horrific three fatalities (two in the Lakes).

Pilot getting “gift-wrapped” due to not catching shoot (during SIV)

A study by Davies et all (2023), which analysed NHS hospital admissions 2012-2017, found gliding (PG & HG) had an incidence rate of 191 per 100,000 hours. Whilst 3rd highest, it is well behind motorsports (532) and just below equestrian (235). Now I don't hear very many people calling horse people “extreme” (a high proportion of their accidents apparently are road traffic related due to too fast/close passing, but then the wind is also an ‘external factor’ to us).

 An article in the FAI magazine 2006 reported a 1.3-2% number of accidents per pilot per year for 2003-2004. And, probably best known as many of you may well have participated, a survey by Wilkes et all (2021) of active PG pilots estimated ~1.4 deaths and ~20 serious injuries per 100,000 flights (~double that of both general aviation and sky diving).

The Wilkes’ survey found serious incidents in paragliding are (surprise surprise) overwhelmingly due to irretrievable ‘departures from normal flight’ (“typically asymmetry and rotational forces leading to incidents with limb and back injuries”), with only 0.6% due to equipment failure, and then pilots failing to throw their reserves quick enough or at all.

The key word here is “irretrievable”: The question is not IF but WHEN you will encounter said ‘departure from normal flight’. Learning to read the terrain and the air to reduce the likelihood of being ‘in the wrong place at the wrong time’ should reduce the probability, but practise your recovery methods.  Don’t rely on “hands up” because you fly a “safe” wing. If anything, know how to catch the wing when it shoots to avoid a tumble into the lines. Timing is everything!  If not already done (and you didn’t learn to fly on those highly-unstable wings a few decades ago which I'm sure quickly and deeply ingrained wing control), doing an SIV is strongly recommended by most.
If you don’t “immediately” get back in control, throw the reserve promptly: “If in doubt, throw it out”.

Further, a larger and I'm convinced massively under-reported number of incidents, albeit mostly (but not all) less serious, occur during take-off and landing: The number one, and so easy to do, mitigation here is to practise your wing control skills by ground handling lots and lots. Finding yourself flying in increasing wind and having to land vertically or even backward is not the time to figure out how to do a C-riser slam on touch down. Instead of just para-waiting when it is “just too light” or “high end”, use those times to practise your GH skills. I have personally found great benefit (and fun) in trying to see how long I can keep my wing up in very light conditions. Practising GH in high conditions (away from take off on a flat area) ingrains the skills you will occasionally need to land safely.

 

Brain feed: Whilst we’re flying very little now we’re in the depths of winter, remember that your brain does not know the difference between reality and visualisation or simulation/gaming. Use that to visualise your flying objectives, be it emergency manoeuvres, catching that next thermal or nailing that takeoff and landing. Visualise it with your eyes closed and go through it in detail. You’ll be better prepared come spring (or that mid-winter) flight.

The FAI article sums it nicely: Knowledge, skills and attitude are key ingredients to make the sport safer. It is about you as an individual. Even though this is a dangerous sport, if you exercise your new skills and avoid allowing your ego to stop you from making rational decisions, you can decrease the risks a lot.

Last season my personal objective, following my crash late ‘24, was to “take it easy”. Interestingly enough, eliminating the addictive “must-fly” mind-set meant I actually became more relaxed, better at wing control and still saw me fly my way to a new PB (just) and my next XC mug.  My objective for 2025 non-XC days is to practise and try to get at reasonably decent at moderate wing-overs, that culmination of smooth wing control.

Wishing you a great 2026: Fly safe, fly far !

sections.title: Club Nights 2026
sections.content:
Mike Barker, Social Secretary reports

Following feedback from the AGM, we’ll be introducing a new format for Club Nights from 2026.

  • Pre-drinks and parachat: from 7:00pm in the function room (not the bar area).
    Giving new members a better opportunity to meet/socialise & avoids disturbing live music in the bar.
  • Presentations will start promptly at 7:30pm.
  • Presentation length: no more than 90 minutes.
  • Any off-topic interjections will be saved for after the presentation.

These changes should allow for an earlier finish for those with long journeys home, while also creating more time afterwards for socialising and informal conversation.

We hope this encourages back those members who felt evenings were running too long, and helps make the club even more welcoming to new members.

The Horse & Farrier once again have hot food available and continue to provide their function room free of charge, so please do thank them and be courteous to the staff.

Next Club Night - Thursday 8th January – Our very own Richard Meek, British Team Pilot and Manager and 2 times XC League Winner will be presenting from 7:30pm on Task Planning and Setting, Team Flying, and Using Forecasting Sites Effectively.

Happy New Year and Safe Flying

Dates for your diary

Thursday 5th February – British Paragliding Champion Richard Butterworth on his comp season of 2025 and the highs and lows of flying the PWC China and British Championships Macedonia

Thursday 5th March – Andrew Beevers of the DSC presenting on using forecasting tools to plan an XC, great timing for early March!

sections.title: The Mark Sellern Trophy
sections.content:
Martin Baxter reports

Photo: Mark Sellern Trophy.

I’ve always had mixed feelings about this trophy.  It’s certainly very impressive but, weighing more than 21kg and standing 2 feet tall with a similar wingspan, it’s not the easiest thing to move around or display in your average home.  In the past I’ve even been mercenary enough to suggest that we should sell it for scrap, but research revealed that bronze is only worth about £4 per kg.

This is what is says in the club archives:  

‘The Mark Sellen Trophy is awarded for Services to the Club and is generally awarded to a retiring committee member or someone who has contributed outstanding service. It’s one of our most distinctive trophies – being a 2ft high bronze bird/hang glider and a crane is required to lift it. Mark’s family very kindly commissioned the trophy after he was killed out in Slovakia whilst competing in the Victoria Cup on his paraglider in August 1998.’

I believe that, using the money donated by Mark’s family, club member Kate Maddision was commissioned to design the trophy.  Kate died in 2020.  Whilst it is normally presented to a committee member (you’d be hard pressed to do more for the club than they do), we did once present it to farmer Cliff Allen, who had been a great supporter of the club before he succumbed to MND.

Following the last AGM, our Trophies Officer, Richard Meek, took pity on me and gave me the option NOT to take it home. I was sorely tempted, but it’s an honour to be the recipient, and besides I’m far too vain; so I ferried it down the stairs at the Horse & Farrier, and out to the car in 2 trips, with some suspicious looks from the participants at the live mike night.  The next morning my car’s rear suspension breathed a sigh of relief when I relieved it of its load, but I then faced the bigger challenge of negotiating with ‘er indoors to find a suitable location to display it for the next 12 months.

Photo: original wing contrasting with polished base.
One of the problems with such a big chunk of metal is that when you bring it in from the cold (loft, car, garage, etc) it acts as a heat sink, and water moisture quickly condenses onto the surface leading to tarnishing.  I killed 2 birds with one stone.  Mrs B was delighted when I transported the trophy out to the garage, where I was then able to while away a few hours armed with an electric drill, polishing attachments and copious quantities of chrome polish.

Photo: before and after.

I’d particularly like to thank a previous (unidentified) recipient who tried to glue the copper collar to the wooden base, failing to appreciate that separation is essential for proper cleaning and engraving. (It took me back to Army training and endless hours polishing brasses.)  The glue had long since failed to adhere to the wood, but developed much more of an attraction to the copper.  It took me bloody ages to get it off, first using a chisel, then a scraper and various grades of Emery cloth.

Photo: chiselling off the old glue.

It came up rather well and, having spent so much time getting to know its intimate nooks and crannies, I have to say that we bonded rather well.  I now find the lines aesthetically pleasing and have grown quite attached to it.

Photo: restored to its former glory; aesthetically pleasing.

We’ve even found a place for it to reside – in our cottage in Hawes: arguably the epi-centre of the club’s flying exploits.
